previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of paraplegia, neurogenic bladder, diabetes, and chronic constipation was admitted for left flank pain and abdominal distension. Initial concern was for urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis, but she remained afebrile with no leukocytosis, and urine cultures showed contamination with fecal flora. Imaging revealed significant fecal loading without obstruction. She was treated for bowel impaction with an aggressive bowel regimen, reduction of opioid analgesics, and manual disimpaction, which led to improved pain and distension. Blood glucose was managed with dietary changes and insulin adjustments. Her condition stabilized, and she was deemed ready for discharge, but she left against medical advice before receiving formal discharge instructions or medications.

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient is an ___ year old female with PMH of polysubstance 
abuse, poorly controlled DM2, spinal paralysis secondary to a 
gun shot wound, wheelchair bound with a neurogenic bladder, 
indwelling Foley, and bowel incontinence, who presented with 
left sided flank/abdominal pain similar to prior admissions.
.
# Abdominal Pain: There was initial concern for pyelonephritis 
given her flank pain.  However, given her unrevealing UA, normal 
white count, and lack of fevers, her pain was more likely due to 
constipation exacerbated by dehydration, immobility, poor diet, 
and narcotic abuse.  While admitted, she refused a significant 
part of her bowel regimen and did not have a bowel movement.  
She maintained good PO intake and her pain was well controlled 
with low doses of Acetaminophen alone.
.
# DVT/PE History: She has a right DVT documented on US ___ 
with possible extension into pelvis.  She complained of lower 
extremity swelling on admission, but there were no symptoms of a 
new PE.  Medical record suggests long history of noncompliance 
with her anticoagulation regimen, and patient reports recent 
noncompliance with all medications.  Anticoagulation was started 
on admission with Coumadin, and Lovenox for bridging her to a 
therapeutic INR.  The risks posed by her DVT, including PE and 
sudden death, and the importance of anticoagulation were 
discussed in detail with the patient.  It was recommended that 
she start outpatient treatment with Coumadin, and the need for 
close outpatient monitoring to avoid serious bleeding 
complications was also discussed in detail.  She agreed to start 
Coumadin and follow up after discharge with her PCP and the ___ 
___ for INR monitoring.  She was prescribed enough 
Coumadin and Lovenox to reach her PCP appointment, which was 
scheduled for less than a week later.
.
# Diabetes: She is prescribed Metformin, but had not been taking 
any of her medications.  She claims to have been on sliding 
scale Insulin in the past, but reported that she did not bother 
checking her fingersticks.  She was kept on a Humalog sliding 
scale while admitted and prescribed Metformin and Glipizide at 
discharge.
.
# Right Thigh Decubitus Ulcer: On admission, she was found to 
have a stage 2 decubitus ulcer on the flexor surface of her 
right thigh, most likely due to pressure from her wheel chair.  
The wound was monitored and treated with standard wound care 
procedures.
.
# Depression: She reported being depressed and that depression 
was one of the reasons she was noncompliant with medications.  
She denied any suicidal or homicidal ideation, and did not show 
any evidence of psychotic features.  She does not have a 
therapist or psychiatrist, and reports that her depression was 
previously managed in primary care.  She was prescribed 
Fluoxetine, but has not been taking it, and has not seen her 
primary care doctor in several years.  She was offered 
antidepressants and further psychiatric evaluation, but 
declined.  She will need close followup of her depression as an 
outpatient considering the impact it may be having on her 
overall health through medication noncompliance.
.
# Polysubstance abuse: She has a long history of substance abuse 
with crack cocaine, alcohol, and marijuana.  She did not show 
any evidence of intoxication or withdrawal during her admission. 
 She was given Thiamine, Folic acid, and a Multivitamin while an 
inpatient.  She was monitored on a CIWA scale, but did not 
require medication.  She was kept on a Nicotine patch during her 
stay.
.  
# Pruritic rash:  On admission, she had multiple pruritic 
papules on her back, abdomen, and extremities consistent with 
bed bug bite lesions.  Given her lack of interdigital lesions 
and linear markings, scabies were unlikely.  Her pruritus was 
controlled symptomatically with Sarna lotion and Benadryl.
.
# Dispo: Multiple long discussions were held with the patient 
regarding the need for medication compliance and medical 
followup, particularly regarding her need for anticoagulation.  
On the day of discharge, she agreed to start Coumadin and adhere 
to the proposed followup plan.  Case management started the 
process of procuring her medications given her financial need 
and the high cost of Lovenox.  She became impatient while her 
discharge planning was being completed and the Lovenox scripts 
were being processed.  She said that her scripts could be sent 
to ___, that her brother would pay for the medications, 
and that she did not want to wait.  Her discharge instructions 
were finalized and a discharge order was placed, but she left 
AMA before being given her discharge papers.
.
The particular pharmacy she uses was not listed, so the scripts 
were faxed to the ___ nearest her recorded address.  They 
were later faxed to the ___ pharmacy where she receives much of 
her care.  A message was left at her emergency contact number by 
one of the house officers regarding the importance of keeping 
her appointments.
.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital for abdominal pain, which was 
most likely due to constipation.  You were started on an 
aggressive bowel regimen to help relieve your constipation, as 
well as anti-nausea medication.  You should continue your bowel 
regimen to treat your constipation and avoid similar 
constipation in the future.
.
Because of the blood clots in your leg veins, it is very 
important that you take Coumadin to thin your blood.  Not taking 
Coumadin puts you at risk for the blood clots going to your 
lungs, which could potentially be fatal.  You will need to have 
close followup after discharge to adjust your dosage of Coumadin 
to the proper level.  Taking Coumadin without this followup 
could lead to excessively high levels of the drug and serious 
bleeding in your digestive tract or brain.  While your Coumadin 
dose is being adjusted, you should take Lovenox injections twice 
daily.
.
For your diabetes, you should start taking Metformin and 
Glipizide.  Insulin is not recommended at this time.  
Prescriptions for these medications have been provided for you.
